Primer 1 left you with vectors. Stand several equal-length vectors side by side
and you have the rectangle you will analyse: **one row per observation**, such as
a person, a household or a notification, and **one column per variable**. In the
tidyverse that rectangle is a **tibble**.

## Building a tibble

`tibble()` takes named vectors and lines them up as columns. Each one must be
the same length.

```{webr}
library(tibble)

participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

participants
```

Read the header it printed. `# A tibble: 5 × 5` is 5 rows by 5 columns, and
under each column name sits its type: `<chr>` for text, `<dbl>` for a number
with decimals, `<lgl>` for `TRUE`/`FALSE`. A plain `data.frame` tells you none
of that until you ask.

::: {.callout-note}
## Know what one row represents
Many "how do I do X in R" problems turn out to be data in the wrong shape. If a person appears on 3 rows because they had 3 visits, the observation
is a *visit*, not a person. That is fine, as long as you know it and say it.
Confusion starts when you cannot say what one row is.
:::

## Looking at one

4 functions. Use them on every dataset you open, before anything else.

```{webr}
library(tibble)
participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

nrow(participants)      # how many rows
ncol(participants)      # how many columns
names(participants)     # what the columns are called
str(participants)       # types and the first few values
```

`summary()` is the fifth, and it is worth the extra second:

```{webr}
library(tibble)
participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

summary(participants)
```

A minimum age of 3, or a blood pressure of 0, shows up here and nowhere else
until it has already ruined an analysis.

## Getting a column out

`$` unwraps one column back into the vector it was.

```{webr}
library(tibble)
participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

participants$age
mean(participants$sbp)
```

That is the pattern: a tibble is a bundle of vectors, and `$` gets one.

Everything you learned in Primer 1 now applies to a real dataset:

```{webr}
library(tibble)
participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

# What proportion are smokers? A logical column sums as 1s and 0s.
mean(participants$smoker)

# How many have systolic BP of 140 or more?
sum(participants$sbp >= 140)
```

## Counting a categorical variable

`table()` is base R and it is still the fastest way to see what is in a column.

```{webr}
library(tibble)
participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

table(participants$district)
```

Cross two columns and you have the beginning of a 2×2 table, which is where
Primer 7 starts:

```{webr}
library(tibble)
participants <- tibble(
  id       = c("P01", "P02", "P03", "P04", "P05"),
  district = c("Kolar", "Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan", "Tumkur"),
  age      = c(34, 51, 22, 67, 45),
  smoker   = c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE),
  sbp      = c(128, 142, 118, 156, 134)
)

table(participants$smoker, participants$sbp >= 140)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `table()` drops missing values silently
By default `table()` does not count `NA`s and does not tell you it left them
out. Your percentages then quietly refer to a smaller denominator than you
think. Use `table(x, useNA = "ifany")` whenever the column might have holes.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: build a tibble"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Three villages were surveyed for anaemia. Kolar screened 120 women and found
44 anaemic; Tumkur screened 95 and found 28; Hassan screened 140 and found 61.

Put this into a tibble called `survey` with three columns: `village`,
`screened` and `anaemic`, in that order.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tibble
survey <- tibble(
  village  = ______,
  screened = ______,
  anaemic  = ______
)

survey
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tibble
#| solution: true
survey <- tibble(
  village  = c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan"),
  screened = c(120, 95, 140),
  anaemic  = c(44, 28, 61)
)

survey
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_tibble
#| check: true
expected <- tibble::tibble(
  village  = c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan"),
  screened = c(120, 95, 140),
  anaemic  = c(44, 28, 61)
)
# A data.frame answer is just as correct as a tibble one, so normalise first.
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.data.frame(.result), as.data.frame(expected),
                     check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct: three rows, three columns, one row per village.")
} else if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is not a table yet. Use tibble() with three named columns.")
} else if (ncol(.result) != 3) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You need exactly three columns: village, screened and anaemic.")
} else if (nrow(.result) != 3) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You need one row per village, so three rows.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Check the spelling and the order. Kolar first, then Tumkur, then Hassan, with each village's own two numbers.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_tibble"}
Each column is its own vector, so each needs its own `c()`. The village names
are text and need quotation marks; the counts are numbers and do not.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: prevalence from a column"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Using `survey`, compute the **overall** prevalence of anaemia across all three
villages: total anaemic divided by total screened, as a proportion rounded to
three decimal places.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_prev
survey <- tibble(
  village  = c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan"),
  screened = c(120, 95, 140),
  anaemic  = c(44, 28, 61)
)

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_prev
#| solution: true
survey <- tibble(
  village  = c("Kolar", "Tumkur", "Hassan"),
  screened = c(120, 95, 140),
  anaemic  = c(44, 28, 61)
)

round(sum(survey$anaemic) / sum(survey$screened), 3)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_prev
#| check: true
# 133 anaemic out of 355 screened = 0.3746...
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.375))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 133 of 355, so 37.5%. Note this is NOT the average of the three village prevalences; the villages are different sizes.")
} else if (length(.result) == 3) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Those are the three village prevalences. The overall figure needs the totals: sum the numerators and sum the denominators first.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.366, tolerance = 2e-3))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the unweighted mean of the three village prevalences. It gives Tumkur's 95 women the same weight as Hassan's 140. Divide total anaemic by total screened instead.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. You want sum(survey$anaemic) / sum(survey$screened), rounded to 3 places.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Pull each column out with $, sum it, divide one total by the other, then round to 3.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_prev"}
`survey$anaemic` gives you the three counts. `sum()` adds them. Do the same for
`screened`, divide, then `round(..., 3)`.
:::
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Build a tibble from named, equal-length vectors.
- Say what one row of any dataset represents, before you analyse it.
- Look at a new dataset with `nrow`, `names`, `str` and `summary`.
- Pull a column out with `$` and use everything from Primer 1 on it.
- Count categories with `table()`, and remember that it hides `NA` by default.
- See why an overall proportion is not the average of group proportions.
